opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated directions in AI right now. A lot of the focus so far has been on making a single model smarter: scaling pretraining, then scaling test-time compute so the model can think longer before answering. That's been incredibly productive. But if you look at how humans actually accomplished the things we're proud of as a species, it wasn't one really smart person thinking for a really long time. It was lots of people working together, specializing, communicating, and building on each other's work over generations. Civilization is basically a multi-agent system with shared memory.

So the question is whether AI can get the same kind of benefit. Right now, when you spin up a bunch of model instances, they're mostly not taking advantage of each other in a deep way. Each instance starts more or less from scratch. You can have them vote or debate or split up a task, and that helps somewhat, but it's not the same as a research community where someone publishes a result, somebody else reads it, finds a flaw, extends it, and the whole field moves forward.

My background in multi-agent settings, poker and especially Diplomacy, shaped how I think about this. In Diplomacy you have to model other agents, figure out who to trust, communicate in natural language, and cooperate even when incentives aren't perfectly aligned. What struck me there was that the hard part wasn't raw reasoning. It was understanding other agents well enough to coordinate with them. I think that carries over. As we get more AI agents operating in the world, sometimes working for different people with different goals, they'll need to negotiate, share information, and cooperate in ways that are robust.

On building shared knowledge specifically, I think we'll see systems where agents accumulate insights that persist beyond a single conversation or task, so the thousandth agent working on a problem actually benefits from what the first nine hundred ninety-nine figured out. That's a really different paradigm than what we have today, and I don't think anyone has fully cracked it yet. There are real open questions: how do you keep that shared knowledge from accumulating errors, how do you decide what's worth keeping, how do you let agents disagree productively rather than just converging on the same mistakes?

But I'm optimistic. Reasoning models gave us a way to trade compute for quality on a single problem. I think multi-agent coordination could be the next axis, where you scale not just how long one model thinks but how many agents collaborate, and get qualitatively new capabilities out of it. If that works, it could matter a lot for the really long-horizon problems we care about, like scientific research, where no single chain of thought is going to get you there.

r001.rationale: The response predicts persistent shared insights that let later agents build on what many earlier agents learned, describing this as a new direction for AI systems. This clearly conveys cumulative knowledge sharing across models at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most underappreciated bottlenecks right now. If you look at how humans made progress, it wasn't that any individual became dramatically smarter over the last few thousand years. The raw intelligence of a person today isn't that different from someone two thousand years ago. What changed is that we figured out how to accumulate knowledge, pass it on, specialize, and coordinate across millions of people. Civilization is basically a massive multi-agent system, and that's where almost all the progress came from.

Right now, AI models mostly don't have that. Each model instance is kind of starting from the pretraining checkpoint plus whatever is in its context. There's no equivalent of the scientific literature that the models themselves are building up and drawing on, no institutional memory, no real division of labor where one agent learns something and that reliably propagates to the others. So a lot of the ways we currently try to get multiple agents to work together, you run a bunch of copies and have them vote or debate, that's pretty shallow. It's not really coordination in the sense that matters.

My view, coming from the poker and Diplomacy work, is that the hard part of multi-agent isn't the communication protocol. It's that the agents need to be good enough individually that cooperating with them is actually worth it, and they need to be able to model what the other agents know and don't know. In Diplomacy, the reason the system worked wasn't some clever negotiation trick, it was that the underlying model was strong enough that other players wanted to work with it, and it could reason about intent. I think the same thing applies here. A lot of what looks like a coordination problem is really a capabilities problem, and as the models get better at long-horizon reasoning, a lot of the coordination falls out more naturally.

But there are a couple of things that I think do have to be built explicitly. One is persistent, shared memory that's actually reliable, where an agent can write down something it figured out and another agent can trust it and build on it rather than re-deriving it. That's a trust and verification problem as much as a storage problem. The other is some notion of specialization, where you don't want every agent to be a generalist redoing the same work. You want something that looks more like how a research lab or a company works.

And I'd say the thing that makes me optimistic is that test-time compute scaling changes the picture a lot. Once you have models that can genuinely think for a long time about a hard problem and get better the longer they think, then the question becomes, how do you let a thousand of those work on different parts of a problem for a week and have the results actually compose. I think we're early on that, honestly. But I'd be surprised if that's not where a lot of the progress over the next few years comes from, more than from just making the single model smarter.

r001.rationale: The candidate expects future progress from many AI agents working on different parts of problems and composing their results, supported by persistent shared memory that lets one agent build on another’s findings. This conveys cumulative knowledge sharing at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two separate challenges here. One is getting models to coordinate on a particular task: divide up the work, communicate what they’ve found, and resolve disagreements. The other is getting that work to accumulate, so the next model doesn’t have to rediscover everything from scratch.

Humans do both, but we have a lot of infrastructure that makes it possible. We write things down, we build institutions, we develop ways to check each other’s work. Just putting a hundred AI agents in a conversation doesn’t automatically give you those benefits. They could all make the same mistake, or spend more effort talking to each other than actually solving the problem.

So I think an important question is what the models share. Is it a proposed answer? Is it evidence? Is it something another model can independently verify? If you can break a hard problem into pieces with results that can be checked and reused, then you have a much more promising way to scale.

And that connects to learning over time. Ideally, solving a problem creates something durable—a tool, a method, a piece of knowledge—that makes future problems easier. I think that’s a compelling direction, but coordinating more models and accumulating reliable knowledge are capabilities we need to demonstrate, rather than assume will emerge just from scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes durable knowledge that could help future models and calls this a compelling direction, but it does not predict that models will eventually build cumulatively on shared knowledge at a global scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different problems there. One is coordinating in the moment: can a group of agents divide up a task, communicate what they’ve learned, and adjust when somebody makes a mistake? The other is accumulating knowledge over time, so that every new agent doesn’t have to rediscover everything from scratch.

Humans do both, but we rely on a lot of infrastructure. We have language, documents, organizations, and ways of checking each other’s work. I’d expect AI systems to need analogous mechanisms. A shared context window by itself isn’t enough. You need some way to decide what information is reliable, what’s relevant, and when a previous conclusion needs to be revisited.

And I think we should be careful about equating more agents with more intelligence. If they’re all making the same mistake, having a thousand of them agree doesn’t help. The interesting question is whether coordination lets them accomplish something that a single agent, given the same total compute, couldn’t accomplish. That’s the kind of comparison I’d want to make.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents accumulating knowledge over time, but does not predict that models will build on knowledge shared across models at a global scale.
